extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and handling characters in novels: how novels differ from history/memoir, how to treat birth/food/sleep/love/death, the roles of flat vs round characters, and how characters must integrate with plot, point of view, and other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel versus memoir/history
rubrics_metrics.description: A memoir is history, it is based on evidence. A novel is based on evidence + or — x, the unknown quantity being the temperament of the novelist; if a character in a novel is exactly like a historical person, the work becomes a memoir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reproduce real historical people exactly if you mean to write a novel; the novelist must create rather than merely record. The novelist is allowed to go beyond observable evidence by introducing the author's temperament; avoid turning fiction into mere reportage or biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal the hidden (inner) life
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the function of the novelist to reveal the hidden life at its source: to tell us more about a person than could be known from outward actions alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative techniques to expose inner thought, motives and private emotions that history or daily observation cannot supply. This is a chief function of fiction and distinguishes novel-people from historical or everyday people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: thought developing into action (intentionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is fictitious in a novel is not so much the story as the method by which thought develops into action. History emphasizes external causes and fatality; the novel presents existence as intentional and founded on human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dramatizing events, show how characters' inner motives lead to actions; emphasize psychological causation rather than deterministic external forces. Avoid treating characters as mere victims of fate if you want novelistic causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial knowledge / reality by explicability
rubrics_metrics.description: A character in a book is real when the novelist knows everything about it. He may not choose to tell all he knows, but he should give the reader the feeling that the character is explicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create the sense of a fully imagined being: provide enough detail, consistency and plausible interior life that the reader senses the character could be fully explained even if not all facts are revealed. Lack of this feeling risks making characters seem thin or arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of birth in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Birth is an experience we only know by report; in fiction babies often 'arrive off'—introduced perfunctorily and left in cold storage until needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide deliberately how much of early life you will show; while many novelists skip infant psychology, you may exploit birth for thematic richness if you can plausibly render it. Beware the common anti-pattern of treating birth merely as a plot convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of death in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment of death is nourished on observation and often congenial to the novelist; death ends a book neatly and the novelist can imaginatively follow characters through it (but should avoid scraps of séance information about 'life beyond').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use death for powerful, fitting closure grounded in established character and circumstance. Avoid gratuitous spiritualistic or pseudo-evidence about afterlife that breaks novelistic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of food
rubrics_metrics.description: Food in fiction is mainly social: it draws characters together, but they seldom require it physiologically or enjoy it unless specially asked to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meals and food scenes to reveal relationships, social ritual, and sensuous detail when appropriate (poetry has often done this well). Beware neglecting the aesthetic/sensuous dimension of eating if it would enrich character or scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of sleep and dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: Sleep is often perfunctory in novels; dreams are introduced with a purpose and do not attempt to represent the character's full third-of-life spent asleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you depict sleep or dreams, make them purposeful and integrated with waking life; either attempt a convincing reconstruction of dream-life or use dreams selectively to illuminate waking concerns. Avoid treating sleep as mere filler or ignoring its potential psychological weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of love / romantic emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Love looms large in novels—often unduly prominent—because novelists' creation processes and the convenience of narrative endings (e.g., marriage) magnify love's presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of over-emphasizing romantic love to the exclusion of other human experiences; ensure love's role is believable in proportion to characters' lives. Recognize the novelist's own preoccupations can distort characters' sensitivity to love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters often come 'posted' (parcelled into fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in novels commonly arrive like parcels: presented fully-formed, shown to the reader, and then kept until they serve the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept this conventional economy when necessary, but be conscious of its artificiality. Decide when to present a character fully-formed versus when to stage gradual arrival or development to better mirror life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character integration with plot, moral, and other elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must adapt to other requirements of the novel—plot, moral stance, fellow characters, atmosphere—and in complex novels are inter-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave characters into the novel's fabric so they are linked to setting, other characters and plot; avoid isolating a character who should be part of a network (or conversely, avoid forcing an independent character into incompatible schemata). Consider the effects of removing or transplanting characters (it may leave the work deformed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat (type) versus round (complex) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are built around a single idea or quality and can be expressed in one sentence; round characters have multiple facets and develop through circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flat characters for economy, recognizability, and permanence (they need less reintroduction and are useful as fixtures). Use round characters when you need psychological depth, development, and complex interactions; be mindful round characters require more management and integration with the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of flat characters (memorability and convenience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are easily recognized, remembered, and persist unchanged: they 'never need reintroducing, never run away' and provide their own atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ flat characters when you want clarity, immediate emotional recognition, or durable comic/typified effect. Avoid making all characters flat if you need nuance or transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing character autonomy vs authorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may 'run away' from an author's plan if given complete freedom; if kept too sternly in check they may 'revenge themselves by dying' or otherwise destroy the book by 'intestinal decay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance allowing characters enough spontaneity to feel real with sufficient authorial shaping to keep the novel coherent. Watch for characters that derail plot or become inert; adjust either the characters or the structure to restore harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view as a device shaping character presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view is one of the novelist's devices (along with different kinds of characters) that affect how characters are handled and presented to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a point of view that supports the kind of character knowledge you want to convey (omniscient, limited, first-person, etc.). The POV decision will determine how much inner life is visible and how characters relate to the novel's laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality within the novel's laws (aesthetic vs daily-life realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character is real in the novel when it lives in accordance with the novel's own laws; a work of art has laws not identical with daily life, so a character is convincing if it obeys those artistic laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate realism by internal consistency and convincingness within the invented world rather than by literal correspondence to everyday life. For novels where the secret life is visible, psychological plausibility matters more than mimicking life-for-life.
